role: One of the Ten Promised Paradise
Early companion and financier of Islam
summary: Talha ibn Ubayd Allah (RA) was one of the Ten Companions promised Paradise by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Renowned for his extraordinary generosity — earning the epithets al-Fayyad and al-Khayr — and for his singular act of courage at the Battle of Uhud, where he shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his own body, sustaining severe wounds. He is among the most honored Companions in classical scholarship.
biography:
Talha ibn Ubayd Allah al-Taymi al-Qurashi was born in Makkah around 594 CE into the Banu Taym clan of Quraysh — the same clan as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA). He accepted Islam early in the Makkan period, within the first few years of the Prophet's call, making him among the as-sabiqun al-awwalun (the earliest converts). Ibn Sa'd records in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra that Talha was absent from the Battle of Badr due to being on a trading mission to Syria on behalf of Abu Bakr, but the Prophet ﷺ allocated to him the full share and honor of a Badr veteran, indicating his standing.

The Battle of Uhud in 3 AH (625 CE) became the defining moment of Talha's life. When the Muslim lines were broken and archers abandoned their post contrary to the Prophet's command, the enemy cavalry encircled the remaining defenders. In the chaos, Talha placed himself in front of the Prophet ﷺ, using his own body as a shield against arrows and sword strikes. He sustained more than seventy wounds on that day and lost the use of several fingers. The Prophet ﷺ reportedly said afterward: 'Whoever wishes to see a martyr walking on the earth, let him look at Talha ibn Ubayd Allah.' (al-Tirmidhi, Manaqib, with chains assessed by various scholars; Ibn Kathir discusses its transmission in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah). For this sacrifice, Talha was known by the Companions as 'Talha al-Khayr' and 'Talha al-Fayyad.'

His generosity was exceptional even among the famously generous Companions. Classical sources record that after a single trading caravan from Yemen or Iraq would return, he would distribute its entire profit — sometimes described as 700,000 dirhams in a single sitting — among the poor of Madinah, his relatives, and those in need. Al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' notes that Talha left an estate of 200,000 gold dinars and 2.2 million silver dirhams at his death, yet had repeatedly given away fortunes during his life. The Prophet ﷺ called him al-Fayyad ('the one who pours out generously like a flooding river').

Talha participated in the campaigns that followed Uhud: the Battle of al-Khandaq (the Trench) in 5 AH, the conquest of Makkah in 8 AH, the Battle of Hunayn, and the campaign of Tabuk. He was among the six members of the shura council appointed by Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) before his death to select the next caliph — a group limited to those the Prophet ﷺ had expressly promised Paradise, and which ultimately led to the selection of Uthman ibn Affan (RA).

The final chapter of Talha's life is connected to the fitna (civil strife) following the assassination of Uthman (RA) in 35 AH. He, along with Zubayr ibn al-Awwam (RA) and Aisha (RA), traveled to Basra to call for justice for Uthman's murder — a movement that culminated in the Battle of the Camel in 36 AH (656 CE). This is among the most sensitive events in Islamic history, touching the Sahaba themselves. Classical Sunni scholarship holds that all parties in the fitnah era acted with sincere intention, both Talha and Zubayr withdrew from the battlefield before the fighting escalated, and their error — if any — was one of ijtihad (interpretation) rather than willful transgression. Talha was struck by an arrow during or shortly before the battle and died from his wound. He was buried near Basra.

The Prophet ﷺ explicitly named Talha among the ten promised Paradise in the well-known hadith reported by Sa'id ibn Zayd: 'Abu Bakr is in Paradise, Umar is in Paradise, Uthman, Ali, Talha, Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Sa'id ibn Zayd, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas are in Paradise.' (Sunan Abi Dawud, Kitab al-Sunnah; al-Tirmidhi, Kitab al-Manaqib; graded sahih by major hadith scholars).

Ibn Kathir, al-Dhahabi, and Ibn Sa'd all write extensively about Talha's virtues, ranking him among the greatest of the Sahaba. His narrated hadith number approximately 38 in the major collections.
